article_text:
This article appeared in the September 12, 2025 edition of The Film Comment Letter, our free weekly newsletter featuring original film criticism and writing . Sign up for the Letter here .

Cover-Up (Laura Poitras and Mark Obenhaus, 2025)

There’s something strangely sedating about being at the Venice Film Festival. The annual Mostra Internazionale d’Arte Cinematografica takes place not in Venice proper, but on a tiny island called Lido that’s a 15-minute ferry ride from the mainland. For a New Yorker like myself, if Venice feels like a simulation, with its paved, car-free roads, picturesque canals, and historic facades, Lido feels like an idyll beyond the edge of the world. Formerly a “balneotherapy resort” and spa town, the island is suffused with humid languor—even with all the hubbub of the festival, which brings over 100,000 visitors to a community of about 20,000 people, it feels sparse and slow. I listened for the chimes of the church clock to decide when it was time to walk over to a screening. I took naps in my apartment between movies. I cooked my meals with groceries purchased from little mom-and-pop stores once I realized that getting food after 10 p.m. was a near impossibility.

If this is all very relaxing, it is also somewhat numbing, and the awards-aspiring, star-studded, formulaically plotted titles that crowd the festival’s Main Competition don’t help. Be it Paolo Sorrentino’s opening film La grazia , in which Toni Servillo plays an Italian president wrestling with a euthanasia law (and the disapproval of a dreads-sporting Black pope), or Yorgos Lanthimos’s Bugonia , a sordidly unhinged thriller about two QAnon-pilled incel types who kidnap a Sackler-esque CEO, or Kathryn Bigelow’s insipid A House of Dynamite , which tracks the inner machinations of the U.S. government’s war room as a nuclear missile (deployed by a conveniently unidentified enemy) hurtles toward the country, many of the Competition narratives seemed to strain for real-world relevancy but unfolded like playhouse fantasies: broadly characterized, gratingly self-indulgent, and lacking meaningful stakes. (Jim Jarmusch’s Golden Lion–winning Father Mother Sister Brother and Guillermo del Toro’s Frankenstein were two exceptions—the former for its beautifully perceptive and witty exploration of filial ties, the latter for its unabashedly operatic embrace of Mary Shelley’s existentialism.)

Perhaps this is why the films that I cherished the most at this year’s festival were predominantly from the non-Competition sidebars, and nonfictions of some kind or another, piercing through Lido’s illusive bubble with lightning bolts of reality. Exhibit A: Laura Poitras and Mark Obenhaus’s documentary Cover-Up . The movie is about the famed and dogged American investigative journalist Seymour Hersh, although “about” feels like the wrong preposition here. Several of Poitras’s films take off from the life and work of a person—Edward Snowden, Julian Assange, Nan Goldin—but only as a structuring principle to explore ideas and issues of broader social and political import. Her documentaries evade the two grating contemporary trends in nonfiction—the celebrity bio-doc and the montage-heavy issue film—to get at something far more alive and affecting: a sense of how individuals locate themselves within history.

In the case of Hersh, this history is long and difficult. Sy, to those who know him, began his career as a speaker of truth to power by reporting on the 1968 Mỹ Lai massacre in Vietnam, where American soldiers brutally murdered hundreds of unarmed children and adults—sometimes, after raping and mutilating them—under the pretext of fighting the Viet Cong. Cover-Up begins with Hersh recounting how that scoop came about, underlining that it didn’t require much in the way of hardcore detective skills: the facts were there in plain sight, but no one had taken the initiative to investigate or report them. This confrontation with passivity and complicity becomes a through line connecting the many stories—the litany of state-sanctioned crimes—that Poitras and Obenhaus have Hersh walk us through, including Operation CHAOS, the CIA’s secret program for spying on student protesters in the 1960s; the Watergate scandal; and the dark revelations of Abu Ghraib.

Poitras and Obenhaus’s style is simple and direct, and stealthily polemical. Though Hersh’s story is primarily told through archival materials and interviews, we glimpse intermittent scenes of him speaking with a source in Gaza about the killing of children by the Israel Defense Forces; the rhyme with Mỹ Lai is hard to miss. During the interview segments, Poitras’s voice is frequently heard gently probing the prickly Hersh, who is fearful of exposing his sources and hesitant to make a film that centers him instead of his subjects; only briefly does he comment on his personal life, his marriage, or his children. There is a remarkable sincerity in his effort to resist the individualizing and valorizing that reduces historic and systemic struggles to simple, hero-villain narratives—an effort foregrounded by Poitras and Obenhaus’s direction and editing. I walked out of the film in awe of Hersh, but more importantly, reminded of the long fight for justice that precedes our present and must continue unabated into the future.

Lucrecia Martel also balances the long view and the short view, history and the individual, in Landmarks (the Spanish title, Nuestra tierra , translates “Our Land”), her first feature documentary. The film takes as its starting point the murder of 68-year-old Indigenous activist Javier Chocobar in 2009, during a confrontation with police and a landowner attempting to evict members of the Chuschagasta community from their ancestral lands in Argentina’s Tucuman province. Though that incident was captured on video, it took nine years for the case to reach the courtroom; the killers were convicted and detained but released in 2020, due to the court’s delays in considering their appeals. Martel follows the legal proceedings of the trial, which involves public hearings and reenactments. But she is careful to expand her lens beyond this one incident, which, slowed down and complicated by the legal system, threatens to obfuscate the chronic and ongoing injustice of colonialism in Argentina.

Martel and her co-writer María Alché dig deep into the history of the land’s colonization and ownership, detailing the various thefts and sleights of legal hand that form the scaffolding for what may seem like an isolated act of violence. The significance of their approach is illustrated in one crucial moment, when the defendants in court cite an article by a writer claiming that the Chuschagasta community became extinct in 1807. Martel interviews the writer, who is shocked to realize that his work has real-world consequences; he says he just wrote something to “add flair” to an article about an auction, and that if he had to research the pieces he writes daily, he “would die.” At stake is a battle for collective memory, and Landmarks makes clear that archives are structures, designed to privilege certain communities over others.

Some may find the middle sections of the film, in which Chuschagasta community members are interviewed about their family histories, surprisingly straightforward for a filmmaker known for her audacious stylistic experimentation. But this directness reinforces the impression I had of the film at large: that this is a movie invested in committing to the record lives that are frequently, purposefully erased. These scenes are a forceful counterpoint to the official proceedings, where documents, deeds, and laws serve as the means for a state to enforce its hegemony. In one gesture of poeticism, drone shots pervade the film, evoking surveillance, but also the ghostly feeling that the land precedes any of the people we see onscreen—that it stood witness to lives that came before even the state of Argentina.

The violence inherent in the supposedly neutral workings of bureaucracy—its tyranny of rules and procedures—is also the focus of Tunisian filmmaker Kaouther Ben Hania’s The Voice of Hind Rajab , which won the festival’s Grand Jury Prize. Hind Rajab was a 5-year-old Palestinian girl whose relatives were shot and killed by the IDF in January 2024, when they were trying to evacuate Gaza by car. Rajab was trapped in the vehicle amidst their dead bodies and called the Palestine Red Crescent Society from a cell phone for help. The utterly gutting recordings of her conversation with Red Crescent staffers, in which she begs them to come rescue her while they helplessly seek permission for an ambulance to be sent to her aid, form the heart of Ben Hania’s film. The director uses the real audio of Rajab’s phone call, but reconstructs the scenes that unfolded at the Red Crescent call center with actors. The movie unfolds like a doomed chamber drama, where the end comes slowly but surely: the ambulance was mere feet away from Rajab when soldiers gunned down the little girl along with two rescuers.

The film generated skepticism among many critics, and for good reason. Ben Hania worked with Rajab’s mother and family to make the film, and yet, dramatizing the murder of a child—just one among so many that continue to be killed in an ongoing massacre—bears the stink of exploitation, a feeling reinforced by the film’s participation in a glitzy competition at a major European film festival. Many Hollywood stars and filmmakers added their names to the movie as executive producers, including Rooney Mara, Jonathan Glazer, Joaquin Phoenix, and Brad Pitt, which has prompted people on social media to wonder why Rajab’s mother has still not been evacuated from Gaza. I carried these reservations with me into the film, and though the movie didn’t allay them all, I came out genuinely moved by Ben Hania’s approach.

Focusing on a single incident or victim often serves to provoke sensationalistic pity instead of critique, because a limited perspective can obscure systemic injustices in favor of emotionally heightened experiences. But as with Landmarks ’s depiction of the Chocobar case and Cover-Up ’s account of Sy Hersh’s reporting, The Voice of Hind Rajab induced the opposite response in me. The film is sparse and simple, putting us in the Red Crescent call center in real time as the staffers, played by actors, attempt to assuage Rajab’s fears while trying to coordinate a rescue. This coordination is brutally complex: the Red Crescent has to inform the Red Cross, who in turn have to get permission from the Israeli military to open a safe route for the ambulance. Despite the rescuers only being an eight-minute drive away from Rajab, this process takes hours, and then proves to be futile.

This is the terror of the law in plain, unflinching view. In the name of protocol (and what a twisted protocol it is, to have to ask the people shooting up your community for permission to save one of their victims!) governments and their militaries get to inflict violence, so that when they’re called out for it, their response can be that they followed all the rules. I appreciated The Voice of Hind Rajab for illuminating this reality so concretely, and I hope it will affect all of its viewers as viscerally as it did the audience I saw it with. As to its real-world effects, who can say? Cynicism is built into the film, as it is in Landmarks . These movies acknowledge that the modes of resistance available to us, including cinematic and artistic modes, are forced to engage with the same systems that disenfranchise us. They can rarely save lives—most of the time, they can only memorialize them. Whether we greet them with more than just awards and applause is up to us.

爱德华·斯诺登,朱利安·阿桑奇,纳·戈丁 - 但只是作为一个结构性原则来探索更广泛的社会和政治进口的想法和问题。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于那些认识他的人来说,他开始了他的职业生涯,作为一个对权力的真理发言人,报告了1968年美国拉伊大屠杀在越南,美国士兵残酷地杀死了数百名未武装儿童和成年人 - 有时,强奸和折磨他们 - 以战斗越南国会的借口。探偵技能:事實在清晰的眼光中,但沒有人採取開始調查或報告他們. 這對抗與被動和同情變成了一個通過線結合許多故事 - 國家處罰的罪行 - 波特拉斯和奧本哈斯有赫什通過我們,包括行動混亂,中央情務局的秘密計劃在1960年代對學生抗議者進行調查; 華特加特丑聞; 和阿布格拉伊布的黑暗啟示。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "波特拉斯和奥本豪斯的风格是简单的,直接的,和丑陋的争论。 虽然赫什的故事主要是通过档案材料和采访讲述,我们观察他与加沙的一位消息来源谈论以色列国防部队杀害儿童的中间场景; 与美国莱的节奏很难错过。电影集中在他的主题,他只对他的个人生活,他的婚姻,或他的孩子发表评论,在他的努力中,有显而易见的诚实,以抵抗个性化和价值化,减少历史和系统的斗争到简单的英雄和别墅的故事 - 一个努力,由波特拉斯和奥本哈斯的指导和编辑。必须在未来的前进中保持不受打击。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "卢克雷西亚·马特尔(Lucrecia Martel)还平衡了长视和短视,历史和个人,在Landmarks(西班牙标题,Nuestra tierra,翻译为“我们的土地”),她的第一部角色纪录片。电影作为其起点,在2009年与警察和一个土地所有者试图从他们的祖先土地中驱逐Chuschagasta社区成员的对抗中,68岁的原住民活动家Javier Chocobar的谋杀案。案件到达法院九年;凶手被判刑并被拘留,但在2020年被释放,因为法院考虑他们的上诉的延迟,马特尔跟随审判的法律程序,涉及公众听证和重新审判,但她小心扩大她的镜头超越这个一个事件,这,缓慢和复杂的法律制度,威胁要掩盖在阿根廷的殖民主义的慢性和持续的不公正。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "马特尔和她的作家玛丽亚·阿尔切深深深地进入了土地的殖民和所有权的历史,详细描述了法律手的各种盗窃和漏洞,形成了对可能看起来像一个孤立的暴力行为的折叠。他们的态度的意义在一个关键时刻被描述,当被告在法庭上引用了一篇文章,作家声称,丘什加斯塔社区在1807年灭绝。他只是写了一些关于拍卖的文章“添加香味”的东西,如果他不得不研究他每天写的作品,他“会死”。在赌博上是为了集体记忆的斗争,而Landmarks清楚地说,档案是结构,旨在优先于某些社区。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有些人可能會發現電影的中間部分,在那裡丘沙加斯塔社區成員對他們的家庭故事進行面試,令人驚訝的簡單的電影製作人知道她的勇敢的風格實驗. 但這種直覺強化了我對電影的印象:這是一部電影投入奉獻的紀錄生活,經常,故意消失。在诗歌主义的一种动作中,无人机射击破坏了电影,引发了监视,但也引发了地球在我们看到的人群中所面临的幽灵感 - 它见证了甚至在阿根廷国家之前的生命。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "官僚主义所谓中立行动中产生的暴力 - 规则和程序的暴力 - 也是突尼斯电影制片人Kaouther Ben Hania的“印度拉贾布之声”的焦点,该节日获得了大陪审团奖。 印度拉贾布是一名5岁的巴勒斯坦女孩,其亲属在2024年1月被伊斯兰国武装分子枪杀并被杀害,当他们试图用汽车驱逐加沙时。社交从一个手机寻求帮助. 她与红十字会员工的对话,在那里她要求他们来拯救她,而他们无助寻求救护车的许可被发送到她的帮助,形成本汉尼亚的电影的心脏。 导演使用Rajab的电话的真实音频,但重建在红十字会电话中心与演员发生的场景。当然,救护车距离拉贾布仅几英尺,当士兵与两名救援人员一起击落小女孩时。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "电影引起了许多批评者的怀疑,而且有好理由。本·哈尼亚与拉贾布的母亲和家人合作制作电影,然而,戏剧化一个孩子的谋杀 - 只有在不断的屠杀中继续被杀的人中的一员 - 携带了剥削的气息,这是一种感觉,由电影在一个主要的欧洲电影节的激烈竞赛中参与。Glazer,Joaquin Phoenix,和Brad Pitt,谁促使人们在社交媒体上想知道为什么拉贾布的母亲还没有被驱逐出加沙。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "专注于一个单一的事件或受害者往往是引起感性悲伤而不是批评,因为一个有限的视野可以隐藏系统的不公正,以支持情感提升的经历。 但是,正如Landmarks的描述的巧克力案例和Cover-Up的报告,Sy Hersh的报告,The Voice of Hind Rajab引发了相反的反应在我。演员们试图在试图协调救援时缓解拉贾布的恐惧,这种协调是残酷的复杂:红十字会必须通知红十字会,他们必须从以色列军队获得许可,以便为救护车开启安全路线。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在议定书的名义上(和什么是扭曲的议定书,必须要求人们开枪你的社区,以便允许拯救他们的受害者之一!)政府和他们的军队,发动暴力,所以当他们被召回,他们的反应可能是他们遵循所有的规则。观众我看到它与. 关于它的现实世界影响,谁可以说? 愤世嫉俗是构建在电影,因为它是在标志 . 这些电影承认,我们可用的抵抗模式,包括电影和艺术模式,被迫与相同的系统,解散我们. 他们很少能拯救生命 - 大多数时间,他们只能记住它们。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
8月28日に、上野公園の東京国立博物館に新たなミュージアムレストランとカフェがオープンしました。その一つの「THE RESTAURANT 東京国立博物館」では、東博カツサンドをはじめ魅力的なフードやスイーツ、ドリンクが勢揃い。実際に足を運んで、お店おすすめのメニューを注文してみました！

内装は大幅リニューアル、心地よいテラス席も拡大

THE RESTAURANT 東京国立博物館は、同館の正門から進んで右手、東洋館に隣接します。ここにはもともと、「レストランゆりの木」と「カフェゆりの木」がありました。

店内は落ち着きのある空間で、カウンター席からテーブル席、半個室まで充実。内装デザインや座席レイアウトは従来の店舗から大きく変わっています。

レストランを運営するオークスグループは、冠婚葬祭や飲食事業を柱とする富山県の企業で、東京都内でもさまざまな業態の飲食店を手がけています。その経験を活かし、博物館という特殊な立地にふさわしい食を提案しています。

上野の歴史を味わう「東博カツサンド」と新名物たち

お店では、日本で親しまれている出汁や発酵などの技法を使った、和食の“うまみ”を存分に楽しめるメニューが揃います。企画展にあわせた期間限定メニューも毎回登場！

今回は、通年で味わえる東博カツサンド、コーヒーゼリーソフトクリーム、発酵茶をお店の方におすすめしていただきました。

まずは代表メニューのひとつ、東博カツサンドを実食。厚切りのカツは驚くほどやわらかい！富山県産ポークは脂に甘みがあり、さっぱりとやさしい味わいです。カツと調和する蜂蜜使用の生食パンは、ふわふわ食感でほのかな甘みがあり、秘伝のスパイシーソースが穏やかな味を引き立てます。

実は、上野はトンカツ発祥の地。昭和初期から食べられるようになり、喫茶文化のなかでカツサンドに発展したのだそうです。食を通じて、こうした歴史と文化に触れられるのも魅力的です。

オープン当初から好評のコーヒーゼリーソフトクリームは、苦みのあるコーヒーゼリーに、北海道産牛乳の濃厚でなめらかなソフトクリームを合わせたリッチな味わい。こちらも、日本の喫茶文化を表現するメニューです。

大きなグラスにたっぷりのボリュームを楽しめるのはもちろん、「食後に少しだけ食べたい」という要望にも応え、急遽ハーフサイズもメニューに追加されました。顧客の声にスピーディーに対応するホスピタリティにも、お店の思いが感じられます。

珍しい発酵茶ドリンクは、煎茶やハーブティーなどのお茶を発酵させたもので、微炭酸が特徴です。「ワインや日本酒を食事と合わせるペアリングの考え方を、アルコールを飲まない人にも楽しんでもらいたい」という思いが出発点だったそうです。

ロゼワインのような色をしたバタフライピーは、お茶のようなジュースのような、不思議な味。一緒に発酵させたブラックベリーとラズベリーの甘酸っぱい香りが広がります。

鑑賞を楽しむ気軽さとともに、とっておきの美食を

テラス席は本館北の庭園につながる道に面し、緑豊かな環境です。鑑賞前後のランチやティータイムには持ってこい、博物館で過ごす一日を一層充実させてくれます。

同館の新たな顔となるレストラン、THE RESTAURANT 東京国立博物館。その向かいに同時にオープンしたカフェスタンド「GARDEN CAFE」でも、東博カツサンドなど一部メニューを注文できます。9月30日には法隆寺宝物館1階に「鮨会席 おく乃」が開業し、鮨と会席料理のランチや、閉館後も利用できるディナーコースが提供されるなど、博物館の食体験がますます深まっていきます。

展覧会の鑑賞とあわせて、上野ならではの新名物をぜひ味わってみてください。

（ ライター・さつま瑠璃 ）

article_text:
Mexican production company Península Films & Entertainment has boarded “Insectario,” the debut feature of stop-motion animation wunderkind Sofía Carrillo (“Cerulia”). Eduardo Díaz Casanova of Península and Nicolás Celis of Pimienta Films, producer of “Roma,” finalized the co-production agreement at the ongoing 24 th Morelia Film Festival .

“’Insectario’ is a wonderful opportunity to tell a magical story through the unique vision of Sofía Carrillo, one of the world’s leading voices in animation,” said Díaz Casanova.

Related Stories

Where to Buy Tickets for Broadway's Biggest Shows Through 2027: 'Evita,' 'A Few Good Men,' 'Much Ado About Nothing' and More

“The co-production between Pimienta Films and Península Films underscores the power of partnering with like-minded creators to bring profound stories to audiences across borders. We’re confident this is the first of many collaborations to come,” he told Variety.

Now in pre-production, “Insectario” is set in a world without insects, where it follows Lexi, a specimen archivist who accidentally brings a rare, supposedly extinct moth back to life after taking it home from her uncle’s collection.

Carrillo, whose lauded short films such as “The Wandering Witch,” “The Sad House”, “Black Doll” and “Out of Control,” have screened at Annecy, Sundance and Sitges, is hailed by Guillermo del Toro for her formidable talent in stop motion animation. Her credits include Del Toro’s “Pinocchio” where she worked on the puppet costumes.

Her much-anticipated debut feature is written by Monika Revilla, whose credits include “The House of Flowers,” “Someone Has to Die,” “Somos” and “Blade Runner 2099.”

Península, which has also expanded its international presence through its involvement in Killer Films’ “De Noche,” the latest from Todd Haynes (“Carol”) starring Pedro Pascal , joins a stellar group of co-producers, some with Oscar-winning creds: Cuadernos de Cine (Mexico), Valérie Delpierre of Inicia Films (Spain), Daniela Mujica, Productions Ocho (Canada), Matīss Kaža, Trickster Pictures (Latvia) and Hugh Welchman of BreakThru Films (Poland).

Trickster Pictures’ Kaža is the producer and co-writer of “Flow,” Gints Zilbalodis’ animated feature , which won the Lux Audience Award and the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature in 2025. The win made “Flow” the first Latvian film to receive an Oscar.

Welchman of Poland’s BreakThru Films won the 2007 Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film for “Peter & the Wolf.” He later co-directed “Loving Vincent” and “The Peasants” with Dorota Kobiela, two animated features created entirely through hand-painted imagery.

Delpierre, founder of Barcelona-based Inicia Films, has championed the work of acclaimed filmmakers including Pilar Palomero (“Schoolgirls”), Estibaliz Urresola (“20,000 Species of Bees”) and Berlinale winner Carla Simón (“Alcarrás”).

Montreal-based Productions Ocho in 2020 is known for series “Hotel Beirut” and docu series “Kitsch QC.”

Cuadernos de Cine (Mexico) is a post-production house that works closely with Netflix and Pimienta Films, with such notable credits as Gabriel Mascaro’s “The Blue Trail” and Berlin hit “The Garden We Dreamed” by Joaquin del Paso, which competes now at Morelia and is co-produced by Peninsula.

Founded in 2018 by Casanova and his brother Gabriel Diaz Casanova, Península has established itself as a prolific production company in Mexico, developing feature films, documentaries and series with a distinctive creative identity and international reach.

It just launched a new distribution company at the fest, Caos Cine, in partnership with former Pimienta Films distribution head, Regina Serratos.

At least two of the pics it has backed, “The Garden We Dreamed” by Joaquín del Paso (“The Hole in the Fence,” 2021), which premiered in the Panorama section of the 2026 Berlinale, and “Heil Jupiter” by Carlos Reygadas (Silent Light, 2007, Cannes Jury Prize) are competing at Morelia this year.

Another film, “City of the Dead” (“Ciudad de muertos”), a psychological thriller by J. M. Cravioto, held its international premiere at the 59 th Sitges Film Festival .

The foremost showcase of Mexican cinema in the country, the 24 th Morelia Film Festival opened on Oct. 16 and wraps on Oct. 25.

article_text:
One bike, four riders

On July 11 and 12, 2026, the Ducati Bayonne team is competing in the Barcelona 24-Hour Motorcycle Race with four riders—including Thibaut Foray, who lost both legs following an explosion during a military operation in the Sahel in 2022.

To enable Thibaut to take part in the event while sharing the same bike with his three teammates, the Ducati has been adapted to his specific needs.

I spent 24 hours following the team in the paddock, documenting everything from bike preparation, technical modifications, and rider stints to mechanical work, periods of waiting, fatigue, and moments of intense focus.

More than just a story about performance, this series observes the dynamics of a team united around a single machine, featuring four riders with different needs but a shared commitment to racing excellence.

View it online here

This reportage marks the first stage of a project I intend to continue at the Le Mans 24-Hour Motorcycle Race in April 2027.

To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

Good morning!

Acclaimed art historian and former director of the Stedelijk Museum, Rudi Fuchs has died at 84.

The Victoria and Albert Museum is planning to downsize its adult-learning program, the V&A Academy, amid broader threats of staff cuts.

A recently attributed 16th-century painting by Giorgio Vasari, Transport of Christ to the Tomb, will be put up for sale tomorrow in Milan.

The Headlines

IN MEMORIAM. Rudi Fuchs , an acclaimed art historian and former director of the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam, has died at age 84, reports The Art Newspaper, France . Fuchs passed away in Amsterdam on October 25. He is considered one of the Netherlands’ most influential art critics and museum leaders, who ran the Stedelijk from 1993 to 2004, Documenta 7 in 1982, and the Castello di Rivoli , where he was artistic director from 1984 to 1990, to name but a few of his top positions at art institutions. “Throughout his working life, he devoted himself to the visual arts,” his family told the local media Het Parool .

FORCED VACANCIES AT V&A . The Victoria and Albert Museum is planning to downsize its adult-learning program, the V&A Academy , amid broader threats of staff cuts, The Art Newspaper reports. Management at the institution told staff the education program, which has offered expert-led courses for decades, did not generate enough income. However, TAN notes it recorded an increase in sales in 2024-25 by over 22 percent from the previous year, which helped raise its contribution to the museum by over 60 percent to £365,000 ($486,600). Now, the V&A plans to shut down much of the in-person program by the end of the year, possibly laying off 50 percent of the Academy’s staff, according to staff. Other museum departments have reportedly been asked to plan for cuts as well, following strikes over working conditions that are currently suspended . “Nobody had any inkling this was going to happen,” said one staff member. In a statement, the institution said: “We are currently reviewing the V&A Academy offer and the way in which this is delivered as part of wider efforts to streamline activity and identify efficiencies across our operations to ensure they are financially sustainable and deliver maximum impact.” They added that they “are still in the consultation phase.”

The Digest

Transport of Christ to the Tomb, a recently attributed painting by Italian late-Renaissance Mannerist artist, architect, and art historian Giorgio Vasari will be put up for sale tomorrow at the Il Ponte auction house in Milan, estimated at €200,000 to €250,000 (about $223,000 to $279,000). [ Finestre sull’Arte ]

Hillary Clinton visited Naoshima , one of Japan’s best-known art islands, posed with two of Yayoi Kusama ’s pumpkin sculptures, and observed that “in a sometimes dark and chaotic world, art is an antidote to numbness and incuriosity that reminds us the work of creation is an act of resistance.” [ ARTnews ]

The Israeli government has intervened to stop the auction in Norway of a looted Torah scroll fragment believed to have been used by Nazi officers. [ JTA ]

Art Basel Qatar is returning for its second edition, from January 28 to 30 in Doha, with 82 galleries from 37 countries, with the aim to “deepen collector relationship, support galleries, and sustain momentum between editions.” [ ARTnews ]

Three institutions in Turin, Italy ( Castello di Rivoli Museo d’Arte Contemporanea, the Fondazione Merz, and the Galleria Civica d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea ) are celebrating 100 years since the birth of Marisa Merz (1926-2019), the only woman artist in the Art Povera movement. [ The Art Newspaper ]

The Kicker

FIRST WE TAKE PARIS, THEN… After social unrest disrupted Art Basel Paris , cutting it short by two days and forcing museums to close, some are seeing a pattern in escalating tensions around the world that increasingly comprise older art fair structures, reports the Financial Times . While the conflict in the Middle East is on a different scale than what is happening in France, as youth-led protests against economic inequality and poor school conditions continue, doubts are already circulating about the next art-world event: Frieze Abu Dhabi , opening November 19. One art collector said he would be “astonished” if the fair goes ahead “in any meaningful way.” Dyala Nusseibeh , the fair’s director, said organizers are “liaising with the appropriate authorities” on security. With President Trump expected to attack Iran again following the November 3 midterm elections, the outlook is grim. Meanwhile, Art Basel Qatar is slated to open January 28, 2027.

article_text:
Director Ania Winiarska almost gave up on “Good Girls.”

“After six months, I felt like I’d hit a wall. I’ve never had this problem before,” she told Variety .

“It was always very natural for me to gain people’s trust, but my previous films were about boys or men. This one was about teenage girls and even though I’m a woman, I didn’t realize how much shame they carry. I wasn’t prepared for meeting them.”

Related Stories

Todd Haynes, Zhang Ziyi and Daniel Brühl Lead a Star-Studded Lumière Fest Opening With Haynes Teasing ‘De Noche,’ Starring Pedro Pascal

In her doc, premiering at Ji.hlava Intl. Documentary Film Festival, Winiarska enters a Polish correctional center for girls. Some are escaping abuse. Others end up there for skipping school, drinking or dating. Inside, they’re faced with discipline and constant surveillance.

Popular on Variety

“I was just another adult in a very strict institution where they had to obey all the rules and regulations. I think they viewed me as an outsider, but also as someone who was part of the system,” she recalled.

“It took me two years before I could start filming. But once they accepted me, we never had any issues. They would tell all the new girls: ‘She’s good. She’s not a snitch.’”

International rights to “Good Girls” are being sold by Stranger Film Sales. Produced by Story, Film i Väst and Tekele Productions, it premieres an exclusive clip here:

Winiarska, who is Polish, currently lives in Sweden. She was shocked to discover a world that hadn’t changed for decades.

“Most of these people mean well. They try to help the girls, but it’s complicated because this system is so outdated. Rather than trying to catch up with the 21st century, the girls are taught how to cook and sew. Religious classes are no longer compulsory, but they were when I was filming.”

Societies may be changing, but the ideas of what constitutes a “good girl” and a “bad girl” are still prevalent.

“In some countries, and that includes Poland, good girls are quiet and obedient. Certain prejudices are very much alive,” she noted.

“We don’t talk to our children about growing up, puberty or sex education. I was lucky to have parents who cared about me. When I got into trouble, they helped me. If I hadn’t had that, I would probably be one of them.”

Most of her young protagonists don’t even fit the center’s profile.

“Most of these girls shouldn’t even be there. This place is meant for the resocialization of people who have committed crimes or are on the edge of doing so. But when you look closer, you see they got there because they were skipping school, got pregnant or used drugs or alcohol.”

Or simply because they suffer from mental health issues their families cannot or do not want to handle.

“One of the girls suffered from depression that wasn’t properly diagnosed. She was lying in bed for three weeks and her mom, who has similar issues, couldn’t help her. Neither did her school. Instead, the police came and handcuffed her in her pyjamas,” said Winiarska.

“That’s the problem: they don’t recognize their actual needs. I got quite close to the people who work there, and they also admitted they are not trained as psychologists. When you’re not well mentally and you’re are locked up and punished for it, it damages you even more.”

She met girls aged between 10 and 18.

“My daughter is 10. It’s scary to think about,” she said. But sometimes the center can provide some safety.

“Many of them come from neglectful backgrounds and have experienced all sorts of abuse. At least over there they have regular meals, they go to school, and if they feel bad, there’s someone to talk to. They didn’t have that at home.”

There’s another issue, though. Their time at the center restricts their freedom in the present, yet fails to prepare them for the future.

“I only started realizing what’s important in life when I was in my 30s. They leave at 18 with a small amount of money. What are they going to do with it? Some party it away or get pregnant over summer breaks. It’s a vicious circle.”

Winiarska adds: “These girls are strong. They’re funny. But at that age, you don’t understand the world and the world doesn’t understand you. If, on top of that, you come from a disadvantaged family, it’s easy to sink into a big black hole.”

“If this film could change something in our society, it would be so wonderful.”

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "P rem Sahib turns the city inside out, twists it around and rips it apart. His show at the De La Warr Pavilion in Bexhill, a sort of mid-career survey for the 44-year-old English artist, is full of private spaces and urban nightmares that have been gutted and left on display. It’s minimal, claustrophobic, intense stuff."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A sodium street lamp hangs upside down from the ceiling, casting its sickly pale orange glow across the gallery. You feel like you’ve stumbled into some urban back alley where physics has been flipped, it has all the threat of an underpass, but surreal and inverted. article_text:
P rem Sahib turns the city inside out, twists it around and rips it apart. His show at the De La Warr Pavilion in Bexhill, a sort of mid-career survey for the 44-year-old English artist, is full of private spaces and urban nightmares that have been gutted and left on display. It’s minimal, claustrophobic, intense stuff.

A sodium street lamp hangs upside down from the ceiling, casting its sickly pale orange glow across the gallery. You feel like you’ve stumbled into some urban back alley where physics has been flipped, it has all the threat of an underpass, but surreal and inverted. Nearby, three puffer jackets have been squeezed between sheets of glass – are these the blokes who were waiting for you in the underpass? Or are they three strangers who you’ve caught mid-embrace?

That’s what Sahib does, over and over: he plays with the line between terror and pleasure, threat and intimacy, public and private.

So much here is geared towards an atmosphere of discomfort. There’s a deep bass throb echoing out of one space, its tone eventually rising to an ear-piercing squeal, before settling back into a chest-rattling sub. A table has been made out of a grossly overgrown flea’s body, a street sign has been left blank but its light is still on. Two space heaters constantly flick on and ramp up the temperature. It is liminal, weird, uncomfortable.

Queerness is central to Sahib’s work. The double doors you pass as you walk in were taken from a Mile End leather bar that closed in 2022, the water fountain encased in resin is from Chariots sauna in Shoreditch which closed in 2016. Private spaces, places of intimate pleasure, that have been erased from the city.

In one of his signature resin panels, clear droplets have accumulated on a sheet of black aluminium, like sweat gathering on a nightclub wall. You can almost smell it, almost feel hot, damp, writhing people coming together somewhere nearby. Hung up high, two acrylic discs nod to the visual results of rapid HIV tests. There’s intimacy here, but risk too.

Risk, and threat: an obsidian mirror hangs cracked on the wall, burbling out discordant sounds, a slowed down recording of a homophobic rant sent to Sahib on a gay chat room.

Is this all about architecture, as the wall text here insists? I don’t know. Architecture is already about architecture – I don’t need art to make me think deep thoughts about buildings. This feels way more intimate than that description coldly implies. It’s about bodies being pressed together, sweat dripping down a wall, and feeling like it’s all about to be torn away from you.

The whole way through, it’s as if Sahib is asking: what happens when the places that matter to me, where I express myself, are destroyed? What is left for me, for us? Who decides which spaces can survive, who decides what communities are worth preserving, who decides where bodies get to exist?

after newsletter promotion

I don’t think it all works. The recording of Suella Braverman hatefully talking about the migrant crisis that you listen to while looking out at the sea is a bit on the nose, and the little dotty images of the horizon that line one wall don’t really add a huge amount.

But for the most part, Sahib is brilliant, with an incredible knack for crushingly intense minimalist atmospherics. He’s been one of the most interesting artists working in this country for more than a decade now, and a big institutional show like this feels long overdue.

Prem Sahib: Chamber is at De La Warr Pavilion, Bexhill, from 10 October 2026 to 3 January 2027

article_text:
ジブリ作品を通して「禅」にふれる、体感型の展覧会

京都市京セラ美術館 で、スタジオジブリと日本テレビ企画制作による 「禅とジブリ」 京都展が開幕した。会期は12月6日まで。 展示は全5章。前半の1～3章では、スタジオジブリの立体造形や映画の名セリフ、キャラクターに禅語を添えた軸作品などを中心に賑やかに見せ、後半の4、5章では、ゆかりの人物の書画や映像、資料展示などを通し、禅的なものの見方をわかりやすくひもとく。記事ではプレス内覧会と開会式の様子をまじえ、その内容をレポートする。

本展はスタジオジブリのプロデューサー・鈴木敏夫と、細川晋輔、横田南嶺、玄侑宗久ら3人の禅僧による対談をまとめた著作『禅とジブリ』（2018、淡交社）をきっかけに生まれた。

スタジオジブリの作品には、善悪を二分しない多義性、答えを急がない余白、ものごとを分からないままに受け取る姿勢を感じることができる。これは、禅が大切にする「分けない」「決めつけない」「ありのまま観る」という思想と深く響き合うものだという。

本展を企画したスタジオジブリのイベントプロデューサー、橋田真は 「円覚寺の横田管長に『禅とは何か』とお聞きしたところ、『難しいが、強いて言うならあっちの世界とこっちの世界、つまり彼岸と此岸の「間」のようなところをいう』と。ジブリ作品にも、トンネルや扉をくぐってあちらとこちらの世界を行き来する構造のものが多く、とても近いと感じた」。 と、着想の背景を語った。

第1章は「あっちの世界、こっちの世界」と題し、観客は映画『君たちはどう生きるか』（2023）に登場する青サギの出迎えを受け、映画の「時の回廊」を模した空間へと足を踏み入れる。このように本展は『君たちはどう生きるか』の世界観を中心に、鈴木や禅僧らの言葉から「禅とは何か」を問いかけてゆく構成をもつ。

「企画段階で考えたのは、ジブリ映画のなかからいちばん『禅』的な映画をひとつテーマにして、深掘りすることでした。そのなかで、あっちの世界とこっちの世界を行き来する側面が強い本作を選んだ」 （橋田）

映画の世界に没入する、「時の回廊」と「禅の道」

スタジオジブリが手がける展示の魅力のひとつは、その世界観の徹底的な作り込みにある。本章の「時の回廊」も、扉の向こうに「あちらの世界とこちらの世界」を象徴的に扱うジブリ映画3作品、『千と千尋の神隠し』（2001）、『ハウルの動く城』（2004）、『崖の上のポニョ』（2008）の立体造形が配され、ジブリ展ならではの没入感をたっぷり味わえる。これらをのぞき見ながら歩く道筋には、「禅の道」を歩くイメージが重ねられているという。

宮﨑駿と鈴木敏夫。会話に重なる禅問答

通路を抜けるとぱっと視界が開ける。第2章「お茶をどうぞ」へのアプローチ、宮﨑駿のアトリエを彷彿とさせるグリーンの建物が目を引く空間だ。

中に入ると、左手にトトロとサギ男が並んでお茶を飲むカウンター、右手奥の壁には鈴木と宮崎がなごやかに語り合う写真と、その会話からピックアップされた言葉たちが並んでいる。こうしたふたりの会話から多くの作品が生まれてきた。そのやりとりに、お互いが同じ境地に達し、問いを重ねながら気づきを導く禅問答が重ねられている。

橋田は「ふたりは過去や遠い未来ではなく、いまの世界で何が起こっているかを起点に話をしている。耳を澄ませると会話の音声も聞こえてくるので、ぜひ楽しんでいただければ」と紹介。なかには思わず笑ってしまうような軽妙なやりとりもあり、ふたりの関係性がうかがえる。なお、この2章の空間は鈴木のアイデアにより、会期中、少しずつ変化するという。「今、ここ」でしか出会えない展示を楽しめる趣向だ。

禅とジブリが響き合う、絵と言葉の空間へ

続く第3章「生まれるところ」は、書籍『禅とジブリ』の対談から生まれた言葉や映画の名セリフ、「ジブリ禅画」と呼ばれる軸作品を中心に展示。ここに『君たちはどう生きるか』の主人公・眞人の部屋を再現した空間、本作に影響を与えたとされるエドガー・アラン・ポーの物語詩『大鴉』を紹介する空間を加え、3部屋で構成される。

なかでも興味深いのは、鈴木が描いたジブリキャラクターのイメージに合った禅語を、対談相手のひとりである龍雲寺住職、細川晋輔が選び添えた軸作品「ジブリ禅画」だ。

例えば映画『もののけ姫』（1997）の登場人物、サンの絵に書かれた「両忘」という言葉。ここには「ふたつとも忘れる」、「善と悪、生と死などの二元的な対立を超える」といった意味があるという。これは答えを決め切らず問いにとどまるという点で、ジブリ作品が描いてきた、世界との向き合い方に共通する姿勢だ。

映画のラストでアシタカがサンにかけた「共に生きよう」というセリフも、この視点で読むと、禅語の意味と物語がすっとつながって見えてくる。そんなふうに、ここでは禅の言葉とジブリ作品が共鳴し合う様子を多角的に感じることができる。

「禅」の実践と求道者たち。「悟り」とファンタジーの深い関係

第4章「それぞれの禅」からは、禅の世界とその実践へと焦点が移っていく。禅とは本来、余計なものを取り去った「本当の心」を探求する言葉だったという。禅寺では現代でも、修行僧たちが座禅や掃除などの営みを通じて、この道を究めるべく日々生活している。本章ではそんな彼らの様子を紹介するコーナーを設けている。

禅の教えは禅僧だけのものではなく、誰もがそれぞれの生き方に取り入れ、実践可能なものだ。ここではさらに、禅を世界へ発信した鈴木大拙、京セラ創業者の稲盛和夫、江戸時代の禅僧、白隠の3人を取り上げ、貴重な書画や資料とともに紹介する。

本章でぜひ触れておきたい展示がある。鈴木と円覚寺の横田南嶺管長による対談映像だ。

ここでは『君たちはどう生きるか』で、大叔父の言う「愚かな世界」である現実へ戻っていく主人公・眞人の姿が話題にのぼる。そのなかで横田は「禅でいちばん大事にしているのは、悟りを得ることより、いかにそれを忘れ去って現実に戻るかということ」と話し、鈴木も、高畑勲の言葉などを引きつつ、ファンタジーから現実へ帰ることの重要性を語る。 架空の世界で何かを得て、再び現実に立ち返ることこそがもっとも大切だという、両者に共通の視点が示され興味深い。

この時代をどう生きるか。鈴木の書画と言葉たち

最後の第5章では、「この時代をどうやり過ごすか」という題字とともに、鈴木が手がけた書画の数々を展示する。

鈴木はスタジオジブリのプロデューサーとして、高畑勲、宮﨑駿とともに40年にわたり仕事をしてきた。そこにはつねに「書く」行為があり、やがて展覧会の題字などを手がけるようになる。その筆跡には、愛嬌とともに柳のようなしなやかな力強さが絶妙なバランスで表れている。

本章について橋田は「この大変な時代をなんとかうまくやり過ごすことができたらという思いを込めて、禅語をわかりやすく、いまの言葉に直したものや、鈴木がとくに大事にしている言葉を中心に展示している」と語る。

ここでは書画とともに「火垂庵（ほたるあん）」と題された茶室が組まれ、中のしつらいをのぞくことができる。

ジブリ作品というレンズを通し、それぞれの「禅」を持ち帰る

内覧会後の開会式に登壇した鈴木は、宮﨑を評して「宮崎は禅でいうところの『今、ここ』の人。前後を考えない。自分の求めていたものを生まれながらに持っていた。その出会いは大きかった」と語った。過去や未来にとらわれず「今、ここ」に集中することは、禅が目指すひとつの境地でもある。

また本展の「応援団長」であり、映画『もののけ姫』の声優を務めた女優、石田ゆり子とのトークでは、石田の「禅というものを学ぼうという気持ちだったのが、入口のアオサギを見た時から、それを忘れるほど、楽しいことが始まるという気持ちになった。それがジブリの世界の素晴らしいところ」という言葉を受け、「そこから楽しいことが始まるという見方、それこそが禅的だと思うしいちばんいいこと。この展覧会で、それぞれの人が自分にとって面白いものを見つけるようにしていただけたらありがたい」と応じた。さらに「展示から、それぞれが何かを持ち帰ってもらいたい」とも。

禅寺と禅文化が日常の風景として息づく京都で、ジブリ作品というなじみ深いレンズを通して体感する展覧会。楽しみながら自分だけの「禅」をぜひ探してみてほしい。
